AccountBind.description: What the phone sends to bind an ecosystem account; the fields follow the Provider's AccountSchema.
AccountBind.title: AccountBind

AccountField.description: One thing a person fills in to bind a Provider account; declared by the adapter.
AccountField.title: AccountField

ActivityMomentView.description:
One thing that happened to my things.

Facts and names, not a sentence: the wording belongs in the client, next to
the rest of its language, so a Host does not have to know Chinese to be able
to say that an Eidolon was put away.
ActivityMomentView.title: ActivityMomentView

CompanionCreateRequest.description:
Ask for another Eidolon.

``operation_id`` is the client's, and it is what makes asking twice safe:
every identifier the Host derives comes from it, so a retry addresses the
same Eidolon rather than creating a second one. A client that generates a
fresh id per attempt has opted out of that protection, which is why it is
required rather than defaulted here.
CompanionCreateRequest.title: CompanionCreateRequest

CompanionCreatedView.description: The Eidolon that now exists, and whether its memory is up yet.
CompanionCreatedView.title: CompanionCreatedView

CompanionDetailView.description:
One Eidolon, opened.

``is_default`` is here and *not* on a roster row on purpose. A single answer
about a single Companion is a comparison the Host just made against the
Owner's one pointer; a flag repeated across a list would let two rows claim
it. Same fact, and only one shape of it can be self-contradictory.
CompanionDetailView.title: CompanionDetailView

CompanionFaceView.description:
Whether this Eidolon has a face — never the face itself.

A screen asks this before deciding whether a photograph is worth fetching,
and the answer is small enough to ask on every refresh.
CompanionFaceView.title: CompanionFaceView

CompanionLifecycleRequest.description:
Where this Eidolon should be: put away, or here again.

A desired end rather than a verb, so a phone that never saw the answer can
send the same request again — and so a second tap on a button whose screen
had not caught up is a success rather than an error.

Only two states are expressible. ``retiring`` is a step the Host walks
through on the way to archived, not somewhere a person parks an Eidolon, and
deletion is a different conversation entirely: a surface where "put this
away" and "erase this forever" are one field apart is a surface that will
eventually erase something.
CompanionLifecycleRequest.title: CompanionLifecycleRequest

CompanionLifecycleView.description:
Where the Eidolon is now, and who answers for me.

Both in one answer: putting away the one that answers hands the role over in
the same breath, and a client that had to ask a second question would show
"archived" beside a stale answer to "so who talks to me now".
CompanionLifecycleView.title: CompanionLifecycleView

CompanionNameView.description: What this Eidolon is called, after being told.
CompanionNameView.title: CompanionNameView

CompanionRosterView.description: One page of this Owner's Eidolons, oldest first.
CompanionRosterView.title: CompanionRosterView

CompanionSummaryView.description:
One Eidolon, as a list shows it.

No "is the default" flag. The page says which one is default exactly once,
so a client cannot render two rows both claiming it, and cannot disagree
with the Owner record about which one it is.
CompanionSummaryView.title: CompanionSummaryView

ControllerView.description:
One phone that may manage this Host.

No public key. A key is how the Host recognises a phone, not how a person
does — and handing every controller's key to every other controller is
spending authority material to draw a list. The fingerprint is what a person
is shown when pairing, so it is what is shown here.
ControllerView.title: ControllerView

ConversationPageView.description:
When this Eidolon and I talked. Not what was said — that is per turn, and
the Host keeps no words on these rows.
ConversationPageView.title: ConversationPageView

ConversationPreferences.description: Explicit owner choices, stored outside the immutable genome.
ConversationPreferences.title: ConversationPreferences

DefaultCompanionRequest.description:
Which of my Eidolons answers when I did not say which.

``expected_revision`` is not ceremony a client can skip: it is the version
of the Owner it last read, and it is what makes two phones (or a phone and a
browser) unable to both win. A client that has not read the Owner has no
business changing this.
DefaultCompanionRequest.title: DefaultCompanionRequest

DefaultCompanionView.description: Where the pointer now points, read back from the authority.
DefaultCompanionView.title: DefaultCompanionView

DeviceCapabilityRequest.description:
One capability command aimed at a device this Owner holds.

``request_id`` is the caller's and must survive a retry. A slider dragged
across a range is one gesture and several positions; the client sends the
one it settled on, and this id makes sending it twice the same command
rather than a second one.
DeviceCapabilityRequest.title: DeviceCapabilityRequest

DeviceCapabilityView.description:
What the device did, in the device's own vocabulary.

``status`` is a terminal receipt, not an acknowledgement: the command was
already delivered and answered by the time this exists. ``completed`` is
separate from the status string so a client need not know which of a
device's words means success.
DeviceCapabilityView.title: DeviceCapabilityView

DeviceCompanionRequest.description:
Which Eidolon answers through this device, or that none does.

One command with two values rather than two commands: a null
``companion_id`` is "nothing answers through it", which is an ordinary
state and the way back from every other one.
DeviceCompanionRequest.title: DeviceCompanionRequest

DeviceOutputsRequest.description:
What this device may present, decided by its Owner.

No request id, unlike the Companion choice: the expected revision already
makes asking twice either the same decision or a refused one, and a second
idempotency token would be a second answer to the question the revision
already answers.
DeviceOutputsRequest.title: DeviceOutputsRequest

DeviceOutputsView.description:
What this device can present, and what its Owner has allowed.

The two are separate facts and stay separate words: a device declares what
it can do by asserting a Manifest, and nothing it declares grants it
anything. ``allowed`` is null when nobody has decided, which is a different
answer from a decision that allows nothing.
DeviceOutputsView.title: DeviceOutputsView

DeviceRemovalConditionView.description:
One thing that has to become true, and whether it has.

Removal converges across three authorities and this is how it says where it
is: not a percentage, but which specific facts are settled. A condition that
is not yet met is not a failure.
DeviceRemovalConditionView.title: DeviceRemovalConditionView

DeviceRemovalRequest.description:
Take this device off my Host.

``request_id`` is the caller's and must be the same on a retry: removal is
what makes a device addable again, and asking twice must not turn into two
removals racing each other.
DeviceRemovalRequest.title: DeviceRemovalRequest

DeviceRemovalView.description:
Where a removal got to.

``outcome`` is deliberately three-valued: done, unfinished, refused. A
removal still converging is the normal case and must not read as either of
the other two — the Hub, Kernel and the device itself each settle on their
own schedule, and this Host does not stand in the middle pretending it is
one step.
DeviceRemovalView.title: DeviceRemovalView

DeviceStateView.description:
Values a device reported changing on its own, keyed by capability value.

``values`` holds only what was actually observed, so an empty map is a
device that has said nothing yet — not a device set to zero everywhere.
DeviceStateView.title: DeviceStateView

DeviceView.description:
One device this Owner holds, as a person reads it.

Readable and complete, in that order and without trading one for the other:
the top of this model is what a screen shows, and the technical facts a
person may have to read out to get help — the canonical identifier, the
claim's own state, the manifest, the generations — are kept rather than
dropped.

``label`` is derived by the Host rather than by each client. Nobody has
named devices yet, so it is what the accepted Manifest calls this kind of
thing, and failing that the tail of the identifier. It is never invented
into a name.
DeviceView.title: DeviceView

DevicesView.description:
Every device this Owner holds, and what this list does not know.

``coverage`` is said out loud rather than implied by a short list: devices
still waiting to be let in are a different read, and nothing on this Host
observes whether a device is switched on.
DevicesView.title: DevicesView

ForgetConfirmRequest.description: The token the preview handed back, unchanged.
ForgetConfirmRequest.title: ForgetConfirmRequest

ForgetProgressView.description: Where a confirmed forget has got to.
ForgetProgressView.title: ForgetProgressView

ForgetProposalView.description:
What would go, before anything goes.

``status`` distinguishes three answers a client must handle differently:
``preview`` (here is what I found), ``not_found`` (nothing matched those
words), ``too_broad`` (too much matched to show, so nothing is offered).
Collapsing the last two into an empty list would leave a person unable to
tell "you never told me that" from "say which one".
ForgetProposalView.title: ForgetProposalView

ForgetTargetRequest.description: What to forget, in the person's own words.
ForgetTargetRequest.title: ForgetTargetRequest

HomeCountsView.description: How many of a thing there are, split the way a person acts on them.
HomeCountsView.title: HomeCountsView

HomeSnapshotView.description: The registry with what Hub has observed of each device.
HomeSnapshotView.title: HomeSnapshotView

HomeView.description:
What is mine, right now, in one read.

The one call a client makes when it opens. It exists because the alternative
is four round trips and a screen that renders in pieces — and because the
composition needs facts from five places, which is exactly the kind of thing
a Host should do once rather than a phone doing badly.

**Nothing here is invented, and nothing missing is hidden.** Every part is
best-effort: a source this Host could not read leaves its field empty and
names itself in ``unavailable``, so a client can say "the rest of this is
true, and I could not read that one" instead of drawing a confident blank.
HomeView.title: HomeView

HostServiceMutationRequest.description: Compare-and-swap intent, carried unchanged down to the daemon.
HostServiceMutationRequest.title: HostServiceMutationRequest

InputSelection.description: Owner permission to send microphone audio, independent of response outputs.
InputSelection.title: InputSelection

Limits.description: Bounds a real device declares that are tighter than, or differ from, its type's.
Limits.title: Limits

ManagementContextView.description:
What a client reads before it draws anything.

``capabilities`` is discovery, not permission: true means this Host can do
the thing at all, and whether this Controller may is answered per action. A
name absent from the map is one this client has never heard of — a version
skew — while a name present and false is a feature this Host cannot do yet.

``unavailable`` says *why* a false capability is false, for the false names
where there is a reason worth acting on. Two values today: ``not_built``
(this Host's software cannot do it yet) and ``host_not_configured`` (it can,
and this Host was never given the key). A boolean could not tell those apart,
and they lead completely different places — one is a release nobody has cut,
the other is a command somebody can run tonight. A client that meets a reason
it does not know must treat it as "unavailable, no further detail" rather
than as a failure.

``limits`` values may be null, and a client must not substitute a number of
its own: a limit nobody has measured is not a limit.
ManagementContextView.title: ManagementContextView

MemoryCopyView.description:
Everything my Eidolon remembers about me, in a form I can keep.

Not the Host's backup. That one is the palace — vectors and ledgers and the
encoder they were built with — and exists so a lost disk is survivable; only
the operator tool ever holds it. This one exists so I am not locked in.
MemoryCopyView.title: MemoryCopyView

MemoryDayView.description: What it wrote down since a moment the client named.
MemoryDayView.title: MemoryDayView

MemoryLibraryView.description: What my Eidolon remembers, arranged the way it files it.
MemoryLibraryView.title: MemoryLibraryView

MemoryProvenance.description: Known dates and evidence; absent values are never reconstructed.
MemoryProvenance.title: MemoryProvenance

MemoryRoomView.description: One shelf of a person's memory.
MemoryRoomView.title: MemoryRoomView

OwnerNameView.description: What this person is called, after being told.
OwnerNameView.title: OwnerNameView

PersonMemoryDefaults.description:
The Owner's memory policy.

Defaults for future candidates and automatic promotion, which never
rewrite an existing Person's permissions; and whether the household layer
is on: the Owner's default Realm, which every speaker reads and writes
(design §3.6). On unless the Owner turns it off.
PersonMemoryDefaults.title: PersonMemoryDefaults

PersonProfile.description: Explicitly supplied information only; inferred traits need a separate contract.
PersonProfile.title: PersonProfile

PersonaAuthoring.description:
What a person can decide about an Eidolon before it has been anything.

Split from :class:`PersonaAuthoringDraft` so the name is the only difference
between them. That split is what lets this be a *wire* shape: when someone
asks for another Eidolon they already said what to call it, and a request
carrying the name twice is a request that can disagree with itself.

Every field has the value the template would have used, so this doubles as
the starting point a screen shows. A person opening the form sees what their
Eidolon would be if they typed nothing, and edits from there — which is a
different act from filling in blanks and imagining the result.

Deliberately open. These are sentences and lists a person writes, not
validated policy; the canonical genome is what gets validated, and it is
built from this by :func:`build_persona_genome_from_draft` rather than
stored as typed.

character_portrait.default: 一个沉稳、专注、愿意长期理解 owner 的伙伴。
character_portrait.title: Character Portrait

voice_portrait.default: 温暖、清晰、具体，不用空泛语言填补回应。
voice_portrait.title: Voice Portrait

PersonaAuthoring.title: PersonaAuthoring

PersonaChapterView.description:
One thing my Eidolon has been.

No version, no hash, no realizer: those are how a Companion is built, and
what I wonder is when it changed and what changed.
PersonaChapterView.title: PersonaChapterView

PersonaHistoryView.description: What my Eidolon has been, newest first.
PersonaHistoryView.title: PersonaHistoryView

PersonaRestoreRequest.description: Which chapter to go back to.
PersonaRestoreRequest.title: PersonaRestoreRequest

PersonaTraitState.description: An observable evolution coordinate, not a prompt instruction.
PersonaTraitState.title: PersonaTraitState

PersonalMemoryRealmSnapshot.description: Data catalog binding, not a user authorization credential.
PersonalMemoryRealmSnapshot.title: PersonalMemoryRealmSnapshot

PersonalMemoryState.description: Owner management state; never a runtime memory access grant.
PersonalMemoryState.title: PersonalMemoryState

Placement.description:
Which area an Eidolon device (a panel, a BOX-3) stands in.

``device_ref`` is the Hub device instance id (``DeviceRef.device_instance_id``),
the same string the Channel Provider binds a channel to.
Placement.title: Placement

ProviderAccount.description: A bound account, without any credential. ``pending`` carries what is still to choose.
ProviderAccount.title: ProviderAccount

ProvisionalMemoryPolicy.description: Independent Owner controls; neither permits ordinary private-memory recall.
ProvisionalMemoryPolicy.title: ProvisionalMemoryPolicy

RecollectionView.description:
One thing my Eidolon remembers, as I read it.

Text and its evidence travel together. Retrieval scores and internal
routing fields stay in the service; provenance contains known dates and
the user's original words.
RecollectionView.title: RecollectionView

RecollectionsView.description: What it remembers about what I asked.
RecollectionsView.title: RecollectionsView

Refusal.description:
One refusal, in the only shape an Eidolon surface may publish.

Carried under ``detail`` by HTTP surfaces, because that is where FastAPI's
error body puts it and where every client already looks. The status code
still says how to treat the response at the transport layer; this says what
happened, and the two are different questions — which is why a status alone
was never enough to draw a screen from.
Refusal.title: Refusal

RenameRequest.description:
What to call it, as the person typed it.

A name of only spaces passes a length check and would erase the one they
have, so it is refused here — at the boundary they are actually typing into,
rather than two services away where the answer would be the same but later.

One model for a person and for an Eidolon on purpose. The rule is the same,
and two models would eventually make it differ for no reason anybody could
name.
RenameRequest.title: RenameRequest

RevokedSessionsView.description: When every device was signed out.
RevokedSessionsView.title: RevokedSessionsView

Scene.description: Either Eidolon's own list of actions, or a scene a Provider runs as a whole.
Scene.title: Scene

SpeakerExtractionReadiness.description: Numerical extraction readiness; never conversation authorization.
SpeakerExtractionReadiness.title: SpeakerExtractionReadiness

SpokenMessageView.description: One thing said, by me or by it.
SpokenMessageView.title: SpokenMessageView

TaskView.description: Something I asked it to do, and how far it has got.
TaskView.title: TaskView

TeamConflict.description: Owner-scoped locator derived from a still-active immutable run snapshot.
TeamConflict.title: TeamConflict

TranscriptView.description:
What was said in one conversation.

Only what I said and what it said. What tools it called to get there is how
the answer was reached, not the conversation.
TranscriptView.title: TranscriptView

VitalView.description:
One thing about the machine, said the way a person reads it.

``concern`` is decided here and nowhere below. The daemon that reads
/proc knows how many bytes are free; whether that is worth telling someone
about depends on what this Host is for — and this is the layer that faces
the person whose Eidolon lives on it.
VitalView.title: VitalView

VoiceAudioRequest.description: Bounded mono 16-bit PCM at 16 kHz, base64 encoded for management relay.
VoiceAudioRequest.title: VoiceAudioRequest

VoiceCaptureSession.description: Ephemeral microphone grant; credentials must never be persisted or logged.
VoiceCaptureSession.title: VoiceCaptureSession

info.description: The single Owner management ABI. Both management clients are generated from this document; no route here accepts an owner_id, because the Owner comes from the authenticated Controller session.
info.title: Eidolon Owner Management

get.description:
What has been done to my Eidolons lately.

The Host's own record of the changes it made, in the order they
happened. **Recent rather than complete**: how far back it reaches is
how much the Host still holds, and `next_cursor` running out means "no
further back from here", never "nothing happened before".

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

get.description:
This Owner's Eidolons.

There is no ``owner_id`` parameter and there will not be one: the Owner
is whoever this session authenticated. ``cursor`` is the one thing a
client may vary, and it is a value this boundary handed it.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

put.description:
Add another Eidolon for whoever is signed in.

PUT with the client's operation id in the body rather than POST: the
request states an end ("this operation has produced an Eidolon"), so a
phone that lost the answer asks again and gets the same one. A POST here
would make a second Eidolon the normal consequence of a dropped
response.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

get.description:
One of this Owner's Eidolons.

The Companion is in the path and the Owner is not expressible, so the
pair is "this id, for whoever is signed in". One belonging to someone
else answers 404, not 403: an id that answers differently can be probed
for existence.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

patch.description:
Call this Eidolon something else.

The name is the Owner's word for it, so nothing here suggests one,
trims it into a shape, or refuses a name for being unusual. Only a name
that is not one — blank — is refused.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

get.description: When this Eidolon and I talked.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

get.description:
What was said that time.

A page at a time, newest first, so "看更早的" walks back through it.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

delete.description: Take the face away and leave the Eidolon.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

get.description:
What this Eidolon looks like.

A photograph is the one thing on this surface worth not sending twice,
and this is the hop where that matters — a phone over a house's wifi,
not a loopback socket. ``If-None-Match`` is answered with 304 and no
body.

304.description: The face the caller already holds

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

put.description:
Give this Eidolon a face; the photograph is the body.

What may be sent — a JPEG, and not an unbounded one — is decided by the
authority that stores it rather than restated here, so there is one
answer to "is this a face" instead of two that can drift apart.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

get.description: Does this Eidolon have a face, and is it the one I already hold?

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

put.description:
Put one of my Eidolons away, or bring it back.

Putting away stops new conversations from reaching it — the Host will not
hand out a runtime snapshot for an Eidolon that is not active — and keeps
everything it remembers. Nothing is deleted, and bringing it back is the
same request with the other state.

Bringing one back does not make it the one that answers again. That is a
separate thing the Owner said, and reversing it quietly would undo a
decision they made.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

get.description:
Who this Eidolon is now, in the words somebody wrote.

The read an edit screen opens on: editing has to start from who it
currently is, or every edit becomes a rewrite of everything the person
did not retype.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

put.description:
Say who this Eidolon is now.

Somebody describing their Eidolon for the first time will mostly get it
wrong, and a Host that let them name it, dress it and put it away but
never change *who it is* would be withholding the one revision that
matters most.

It appends a chapter rather than editing one, exactly as going back
does — the same act pointing the other way. So there is one way a
persona ever changes, and what this Eidolon has been stays a record.
Saving without changing anything writes nothing.

PUT because the body states an end: send it twice and it lands in the
same place.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

get.description:
What this Eidolon has been.

A record, not a settings screen: every chapter is something it actually
was, and there is no proposal queue here — a Companion considering a
change has not changed.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

put.description:
Make it the way it was then.

Going back appends a chapter rather than rewinding, so the record keeps
the months in between and says when I went back. The answer is the whole
history, because what I want to see afterwards is where that leaves it.

别做了 — stop it.

What comes back is what the Host says the task became, not what this app
hoped: the task's states belong to the runtime that runs it, and it may
refuse because the thing finished while I was looking at the page.

post.description: 再试一次 — ask for it again. The Host decides whether it can.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.
Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

get.description:
Which phones may manage this Host.

Asked by one that already may — the Host never decides on its own who
belongs on this list, and it does not answer to a phone that is not on
it.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

delete.description:
Withdraw a phone's authority over this Host.

A phone may withdraw its own — what it cannot do is leave the Host with
nobody, and the Host refuses that rather than this layer guessing at it.
The answer describes the grant that was withdrawn, so a screen can say
which phone it just signed out.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

get.description:
Every device that is mine.

Composed from two authorities that each keep their own half — the Claim
says whether this device is still mine, the mount says which Eidolon
answers through it — and a disagreement between them is a refusal rather
than a merged row.

The names of the Eidolons are asked for once, from the roster, so a row
can say 由「小忆」应答 rather than an identifier. A roster this read
cannot get costs the names and nothing else: the devices are still
listed, because which devices are mine does not depend on what they are
called.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.
Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

get.description: Read one current device value through the same command authority.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

post.description:
Turn one knob on a device this Owner holds.

The device's own vocabulary comes back translated: a body acknowledges
with words the control layer spells differently, and a client that had
to know both would report a success as an unfinished command.

Whose device this is, whether it declared the capability and whether the
value is in range are all the Provider's to decide — it holds the
channel and the declaration. Nothing here pre-judges them.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

put.description:
Say which of my Eidolons answers through this device, or that none does.

The Host validates the Eidolon against its own authority — one that has
been put away is refused there rather than pre-judged here — and the
revision is the compare-and-swap over what this phone was looking at.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

put.description:
Say what this device of mine may present.

The Host narrows the decision to what the device declared it can do and
refuses a stale revision; nothing here pre-judges either. Allowing
nothing is a decision this accepts — it is how a device is silenced —
and it is not the same as never having decided.

default.description: Any answer that is not a success. One shape for all of them: the status says how to treat it, `kind` says which refusal it is.

post.description:
Take a device off my Host.

This is what makes a device addable again: the Hub refuses to enrol one
it already holds, so a device that lost its own credential has no way
back until its grant here is withdrawn.

The answer says which facts are settled rather than a percentage. Three
authorities converge on their own schedule and this Host does not stand
in the middle pretending it is one step.

What the device last reported changing without being asked.

Only values the device actually reported appear. A missing key means

get.description:
What is mine, right now.

One read when the app opens, composed here because the answer needs five
sources and a phone composing it badly is four round trips and a screen
that renders in pieces.

Every part is best-effort and every gap is named. A Host that cannot
reach its own memory service still knows who its Owner is and which
Eidolon answers; saying so beats a blank screen, and saying *which* part
is missing beats a spinner that never resolves.

``since`` is required. My "today" depends on where I am, and the Host
does not know that — so the client says when the day started rather than

honest — how many memories carry no date, and whether the Host stopped
reading before the end.

get.description:
"你还记得…吗" — the question a person actually arrives with.

Owner-scoped by the session, like every other read here: there is one

get.description:
What has happened here, a page at a time.

The map carries a bounded now — trimmed per Companion so one talkative
body cannot evict the rest of the household — and that bound is a
display decision, not a history. This is the history, and it pages: the
Owner scrolls, the phone asks again with the ``next_cursor`` it was
handed. It is called a cursor rather than a timestamp on purpose — the
page boundary is the Host's, and a client that reads it has taken on a
detail the Host is then unable to change.

The Owner comes from the session, as everywhere on this plane.

Untyped for the same reason the snapshot is: the rows are the contract's
activity shape, projected by the one function that also builds the map's,
so an interaction opened from the history and the same interaction on the
map cannot describe themselves differently.

get.description:
What is happening on this Host, for the Owner asking.

The Owner comes from the session and from nowhere else. The operator
console's Mission Control takes an ``owner_id`` query parameter, which is
right for an operator and would be a way to read someone else's home
here.

Untyped by design: the response is the contract at
``eidolon_sdk/contracts/mission_control/v1/mission-control-snapshot.schema.json``,
which clients parse directly and which the SDK's goldens pin on both
sides. A pydantic mirror in this file would be a second authority for the
same shape.

Every lane carries its own health, so a Host that cannot reach one of its
own services answers with that lane unreadable and the rest of the map
intact — rather than an error that costs the reader everything, or an
empty list that reads as a quiet house.

Owner a session can speak for, and letting a client name another would
create a question this boundary would then have to answer.

post.description:
让所有设备重新登录 — sign every device out, now.

The action for a phone that went missing. Every device has to get a new
session before it can talk to an Eidolon again; they do that on their own,
so this is recoverable rather than a lockout.

It does **not** remove any phone's access to managing this Host — that is
a Controller grant, revoked from the devices screen — and it does not
unpair anything.

put.description:
Make one of my Eidolons the one that answers by default.

PUT, so a phone that lost the response can simply ask again. Nothing
else moves: conversations already running keep the Eidolon they were
started with, devices stay where they are, and no memory is copied —
this changes where *new* unaddressed work goes.

get.description:
What an Eidolon would be if the create form came back untouched.

A form starts from this instead of from blanks, and that is a product
decision rather than a convenience: an empty box labelled 人格画像 asks
somebody to invent a personality from nothing, while a filled one asks
them to change something they can already read. It also makes the whole
screen skippable — "继续、继续、创建" gives the Eidolon the Host would
have made anyway.

Not its own capability. A client that may create an Eidolon needs to see
what it is starting from; two flags could disagree, and "you may create
one but not see who it will be" is not a state worth being able to
express.

Top-level rather than under ``/companions`` so it can never be confused
with a Companion whose id happens to be a word.
